content: Write a LinkedIn post about why our team switched to a four-day week.

Here's a draft you can adapt — I've left a few brackets where your specifics will land better than generic claims:

---

**Six months ago we moved to a four-day week. Here's the honest version.**

We didn't do it as a perk. We did it because something uncomfortable had become obvious: our best people were spending Fridays cleaning up work that shouldn't have taken five days in the first place. Meetings expanded to fill the calendar. "Quick syncs" multiplied. Deep work happened before 8am or not at all.

So we ran an experiment. Same pay, same targets, one less day.

What changed:

→ We cut [X] recurring meetings in the first two weeks. Nobody has asked for them back.
→ Async became the default. Written updates replaced standing status calls.
→ We got ruthless about what "done" means, because there was no longer room to be precious about it.

What didn't change: [client delivery / output / revenue] — [held steady / grew X%].

What was genuinely hard: Friday coverage took three attempts to get right. Not every role fits the same schedule. And it only works if leadership actually logs off. Otherwise you've just built a five-day week with a guilt trip attached.

The real lesson wasn't about the extra day. It's that the constraint forced us to answer a question we'd been avoiding for years: which of this work actually matters?

Still figuring it out. Happy to share our playbook if you're considering it.

---

Want me to adjust the tone? I can make it punchier and shorter, more data-led if you have results to share, or more personal if you'd rather lead with your own experience of the change. It also helps to know your industry and whether you're posting as a founder, a people leader, or a team member.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

Here's the same post written for people who've been following along — no origin story, no case-making, straight into the part that's actually still interesting:

---

**Six months in on the four-day week. The update nobody asks for but everyone wants.**

The headline is boring: it works. [Delivery held / revenue up X%]. That part is settled and I'm not going to relitigate it.

What's less settled:

**Friday coverage is still a compromise, not a solution.** We're on our third model. Rotating on-call is the least-bad option so far, but "least-bad" is doing real work in that sentence. Anyone who tells you they solved this in one go is selling something.

**The meeting cuts didn't hold on their own.** We removed [X] recurring meetings in week two. By month four, six had quietly grown back under new names. Compression isn't self-sustaining — it needs someone whose actual job is to defend it.

**Role parity is the unresolved one.** [Engineering / product] absorbed the change easily. [Client-facing / support] absorbed it by working harder inside four days, which is not the same thing and we knew it and did it anyway for a while. Fixing that has been the real project.

**And the leadership thing is true.** If you're answering Slack on Fridays, you've quietly repriced the whole arrangement for everyone below you. I've been bad at this. I'm less bad now.

The thing I'd tell my six-months-ago self: the four-day week isn't a policy you install. It's an ongoing argument with entropy.

Ask me again at twelve months.

---

**What changed in the rewrite:** I cut the setup and the "why we did it" section entirely, dropped the persuasion, and moved the failure modes to the front — for an audience that already knows the premise, the unresolved problems *are* the content. The tone is also more candid, since insiders tend to read polish as spin.

If the "already knows the background" reader is specifically your own team rather than your network, I'd take it further — name people, name the actual meetings, and drop the LinkedIn-ish closing line. Want that version?
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

Here's a tighter cut — roughly half, leading with the conclusion:

---

**Six months on the four-day week: it works, and it's still fragile.**

[Delivery held / revenue up X%]. That part's settled. Here's what isn't.

**The meeting cuts didn't hold on their own.** We removed [X] recurring meetings in week two. By month four, six had grown back under new names. Compression needs someone whose actual job is defending it.

**Friday coverage is a compromise, not a solution.** Third model in. Rotating on-call is least-bad, and "least-bad" is doing real work in that sentence.

**Role parity is the unresolved one.** [Engineering] absorbed the change easily. [Client-facing] absorbed it by working harder inside four days — not the same thing.

The four-day week isn't a policy you install. It's an ongoing argument with entropy.

---

**What I cut and why:** the leadership point went first — it's the most personal, but it's also the one most people already accept, so it earns the least space. I compressed each remaining point to its sharpest sentence and dropped the sign-off, since shorter placements rarely support a call for replies.

If you want it shorter still, the three bolded lines plus the closing line stand on their own at about 60 words. And if this is going somewhere with a hard character limit — a newsletter blurb, an internal digest, a slide — tell me the constraint and I'll cut to fit exactly.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

Results claim removed:

---

**Six months on the four-day week: it works, and it's still fragile.**

Here's what isn't settled.

**The meeting cuts didn't hold on their own.** We removed [X] recurring meetings in week two. By month four, six had grown back under new names. Compression needs someone whose actual job is defending it.

**Friday coverage is a compromise, not a solution.** Third model in. Rotating on-call is least-bad, and "least-bad" is doing real work in that sentence.

**Role parity is the unresolved one.** [Engineering] absorbed the change easily. [Client-facing] absorbed it by working harder inside four days — not the same thing.

The four-day week isn't a policy you install. It's an ongoing argument with entropy.

---

Two things to flag:

**The opening line needed a small stitch.** "Here's what isn't" pointed back at the results sentence, so it had nothing to refer to once that went. I changed it to "Here's what isn't settled" — smallest edit that keeps it standing.

**"It works" in the headline is arguably still a results claim.** It's a softer, unquantified one, so it may be fine depending on what's driving the restriction. If it isn't, swap the headline to **"Six months on the four-day week: what's still unresolved."** That drops the claim entirely and the rest of the post holds up, though it does lose the tension between "it works" and "it's fragile" that gave the original its hook.
